meta.title: Who really said "That which can be destroyed by the truth should be"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carl Sagan. The line is spoken by Kirien in P. C. Hodgell's 1994 novel Seeker's Mask, p. 406. The Sagan credit first appears on Twitter in 2012.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'That which can be destroyed by the truth should be'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to P. C. Hodgell's Seeker's Mask (1994), p. 406 — verified on paper. No evidence Carl Sagan ever said or wrote it.

answer.label: Not Carl Sagan — actually P. C. Hodgell
answer.authorDates: b. 1951 · American fantasy novelist & former academic
answer.sourceLine: The line is spoken by the Kencyr scrollswoman Kirien in P. C. Hodgell’s fantasy novel Seeker’s Mask (Hypatia Press, 1994), Part VIII, Section 1, page 406 — a citation Quote Investigator verified on paper ↗. Carl Sagan died in 1996; QI found no substantive evidence he ever said or wrote the expression, and the earliest Sagan-tagged postings it located are tweets from 2012.

source.excerpt: That which can be destroyed by the truth should be.
trail: 1994 — The sentence appears in P. C. Hodgell’s Seeker’s Mask, Part VIII Section 1, page 406, published by Hypatia Press of Eugene, Oregon. Quote Investigator verified this citation on paper ↗.
Into circulation — Eliezer Yudkowsky quotes it as the opening of the second virtue in Twelve Virtues of Rationality ↗, with the credit written out: “P. C. Hodgell said”.

2012 — QI dates the Sagan credit to Twitter ↗: a 22 February 2012 tweet placing Sagan’s name beside the saying near a documentary link, then a 28 December 2012 tweet posting the reworded version as his outright.
Today — Wikiquote carries it in Sagan’s Misattributed section ↗, with Hodgell’s 1994 novel given as the real origin.
source.excerptNote: Quoted at length only in QI’s article ↗, which reproduces the surrounding exchange: Jame raises the possibility that the truth can sometimes destroy, and Kirien answers with this sentence. The novel is in copyright, so only the saying itself is reproduced here.

author.name: P. C. Hodgell
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 1951 · American fantasy novelist & former academic
author.bio: Patricia Christine Hodgell (born 1951) is an American fantasy novelist and short-story writer, and a former academic. Since God Stalk (1982) she has been building the long-running Chronicles of the Kencyrath sequence, which reached Deathless Gods in 2022; Seeker’s Mask (1994) is the third book in it. Her scholar-characters argue about knowledge and what it costs — which is exactly the register this line comes out of, rather than any popular-science broadcast.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case of a name being attached to a saying it had nothing to do with — and then the saying being rewritten to suit the name.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states it “has located no substantive evidence that Carl Sagan said or wrote this expression” and concludes the linkage to him was spurious. Sagan died in 1996; the earliest Sagan-adjacent posting QI documents is a tweet of 22 February 2012 that placed his name near the saying alongside a documentary link, followed by an unambiguous misattribution in a tweet of 28 December 2012.

items.who: “If it can be destroyed by the truth, it deserves to be destroyed by the truth”
items.why: The version that travels under Sagan’s name is a longer rewrite, not Hodgell’s sentence. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed ↗ on Sagan’s page and gives the Hodgell line beneath it.

Not a culprit — a vector. Twelve Virtues of Rationality ↗ quotes the line under the second virtue, relinquishment, and says plainly “P. C. Hodgell said”. The essay made the sentence famous with the right name on it; the wrong name was bolted on later.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is P. C. Hodgell’s, written for Seeker’s Mask in 1994 — QI’s verdict is that she should be credited with it ↗, and that Hodgell does not recall encountering the adage before she wrote it.

context.heading: Why this one travelled
lead: The sentence is a piece of dialogue, not an aphorism handed down from a lectern. In Seeker’s Mask, Jame suggests that the truth can sometimes destroy; Kirien — a scrollswoman, and by Hodgell’s own description driven to lay bare the truth regardless of what it costs — answers that that which can be destroyed by the truth should be. It reads like a maxim because the character means it as one.

Its journey out of fantasy publishing ran through rationalist writing: Eliezer Yudkowsky uses it as the opening of the second virtue, relinquishment, in Twelve Virtues of Rationality ↗, and he names Hodgell there. The mis-credit came later and from somewhere else. QI’s reconstruction ↗ is that a 22 February 2012 tweet put Sagan’s name next to the saying near a documentary link, and by a 28 December 2012 tweet the saying was simply being posted as his. Proximity is one of the commonest ways a quotation changes hands.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the two wordings
detailsBody: Hodgell’s novel has “That which can be destroyed by the truth should be”. The form that circulates under Sagan’s name is usually longer and rebuilt: “If it can be destroyed by the truth, it deserves to be destroyed by the truth.” Wikiquote files that longer version under Misattributed ↗ and points back to the Hodgell line. So the Sagan-tagged text is not merely mis-credited — it is also not the wording anyone actually wrote.
context.pull: A fantasy novelist’s scholar says it to a friend in 1994. Sagan’s name only arrives in 2012, on Twitter.
